lead: An addressing mode is the rule the CPU uses to find an operand. The operand is the data an instruction works on; its address is called the effective address. A single opcode such as ADD can take its second value from a register, from the instruction itself, or from memory at an address held in another register. The mode is encoded in the instruction bits. Without modes, every instruction would need a full memory address, and code would be long and slow. Modes let the same operation work on constants, variables, arrays and stack data. Compilers and hand-written assembly choose modes to save bytes and cycles.
prereq: You need: the opcode and operand fields of an instruction from 3.1, and segment registers and memory organisation from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Effective address and the simple modes

blocks.text: The CPU executes an instruction in two parts. The opcode says what to do; the operand field says what to do it to. The effective address (EA) is the address the CPU finally uses to read or write the operand. An addressing mode is the rule that turns the operand field into that address. For a register operand the EA is the register itself; no memory address is needed.

Implied mode, also called implicit mode, has no operand field. The instruction itself fixes the operand. In 8085, CMA complements the accumulator: the accumulator is always the operand. PUSH and POP also use an implied stack pointer.

Immediate mode puts the operand inside the instruction. MVI A,32H loads the constant 32H into A. The 32H is data, not an address. The 8086 form is MOV AL,32H. Immediate operands are fast but fixed at assembly time.

Register mode names a CPU register as the operand. 8085 MOV A,B copies B into A. The data never leaves the CPU, so this is the fastest mode. The instruction is short because only a register number is encoded.

Direct mode, also called absolute mode, puts the memory address in the instruction. 8085 LDA 2050H reads the byte at memory location 2050H. The address is fixed, so the instruction is long. In 8086, MOV AL,[2050H] is direct, but the address is an offset from DS; see the trap below.

Register indirect mode puts the address in a register. 8085 MOV A,M reads the memory location whose address is in the HL pair. The 8051 form is MOV A,@R0: @R0 means 'the memory location whose address is in R0'. The register acts as a pointer, so one instruction can walk through an array by changing the pointer.

sections.h3: Indexed, based, relative and stack modes

blocks.text: Indexed mode adds an index register to a displacement. The index changes at run time, so the same instruction reaches different array elements. 8086 MOV AL,[SI+10H] uses SI as the index and 10H as the displacement.
Based mode adds a base register to a displacement. The base usually points to the start of a data structure, and the displacement selects a field. 8086 MOV AL,[BX+10H] uses BX as the base.

Based-indexed mode adds a base, an index and a displacement. 8086 MOV AL,[BX+SI+10H] uses BX as base, SI as index and 10H as displacement. The effective address is EA = BX + SI + 10H. The worked example below computes it with real numbers.

Relative mode adds a signed offset to the program counter. Branch instructions use it so that code can be moved in memory without changing the branch. 8086 JMP SHORT label adds an 8-bit displacement to IP, and 8051 SJMP label adds an 8-bit offset relative to the program counter. The 8085 has no relative branch: its JMP and conditional jumps hold a 16-bit absolute address, so 8085 code cannot simply be moved in memory.

Stack mode takes the operand from the top of the stack. The stack pointer is implied, so no address appears in the instruction. 8085 PUSH B decrements SP by 2 and stores B and C. 8086 PUSH AX subtracts 2 from SP first and then stores AX at the new [SP], so the word ends up at the address SP − 2. POP AX does the reverse: read the word at [SP], then add 2 to SP.
Some syllabi call direct mode 'absolute' and call register indirect mode 'simple indirect'. The mechanism is the same: the instruction gives an address, or gives a register that holds an address.

sections.h3: The same instruction in three instruction sets

blocks.text: The 8085 has a small but clear set. MOV A,B is register mode. MVI A,32H is immediate. LDA 2050H is direct. MOV A,M is register indirect through HL. LXI H,2050H is immediate because the 16-bit constant 2050H is loaded into HL.

The 8051 marks modes in the mnemonic. MOV A,R0 is register mode. MOV A,#32H is immediate; the # sign means the constant 32H, not address 32H. MOV A,30H is direct; 30H is a memory address. MOV A,@R0 is register indirect. MOVC A,@A+DPTR is indexed: the address is A + DPTR, and the byte comes from code memory.

The 8086 uses brackets for memory. MOV AL,BL is register mode. MOV AL,32H is immediate. MOV AL,[2050H] is direct. MOV AL,[BX] is register indirect. MOV AL,[BX+SI+10H] is based-indexed. JMP SHORT label is relative.

PIC microcontrollers use a register-file model. Most instructions address a file register directly or through the FSR/INDF pair, which acts as an indirect pointer. The idea is the same: the instruction says how to find the operand, and the mode decides whether the address is in the instruction, in a register, or computed.

figure.caption: The tree groups modes by where the operand comes from. The memory branch covers direct, indirect, indexed and relative modes, which all end in a memory fetch, while register mode never leaves the CPU.

spec.aria: A tree groups addressing modes into implied, immediate, register and memory; the memory branch covers direct, indirect, indexed and relative modes.

examples.question: An 8086 system has DS = 2000H, BX = 0100H, SI = 0020H and a displacement of 10H in the instruction MOV AL, [BX+SI+10H]. (a) Find the effective address. (b) Find the physical address. (c) Which byte is fetched?
steps: Write the rule for based-indexed addressing: EA = BX + SI + displacement. BX = 0100H, SI = 0020H, displacement = 0010H.
Add the three values: 0100H + 0020H = 0120H; 0120H + 0010H = 0130H. EA = 0130H = 304 in decimal.
Add the segment base to the EA: 20000H + 0130H = 20130H. In decimal, 131072 + 304 = 131376.
The CPU reads one byte from physical address 20130H into AL.
examples.answer: EA = 0130H (304 in decimal); physical address = 20130H (131376 in decimal); the byte is fetched from 20130H.
examples.check:
DS = 0x2000
BX = 0x0100
SI = 0x0020
disp = 0x0010
ea = BX + SI + disp
pa = DS * 0x10 + ea
print(ea)
print(pa)

traps: In 8086 the effective address is not the physical address. Add DS × 10H after computing the EA. In 8085 a direct address such as LDA 2050H is already the physical address.
[BX] uses DS by default, but [BP] uses SS. Check the base register before adding a segment.
MVI A,32H is immediate: 32H is the data. LDA 2050H is direct: 2050H is an address. Do not swap them.
MOV A,M is register indirect: M means the memory location whose address is in HL. MOV A,B is register mode: B holds the data itself.

quiz.a: The effective address is the address the CPU finally uses to read or write the operand after applying the addressing mode.

quiz.q: Name the addressing mode in 8085 MVI A,32H.
quiz.a: Immediate mode. The constant 32H is part of the instruction.

quiz.q: Why is register mode faster than direct mode?
quiz.a: Register mode keeps the operand inside the CPU, so no memory read is needed. Direct mode must fetch the operand from memory, which takes extra time.

quiz.q: Find the effective address for 8086 [BX+SI+10H] with BX = 0100H and SI = 0020H.
A student computes physical address 0130H for DS = 2000H and [BX+SI+10H]. What did they forget?
quiz.a: The student forgot to add the segment base. The physical address is DS × 10H + EA = 20000H + 0130H = 20130H, not 0130H.

quiz.q: 8051 instruction MOVC A,@A+DPTR: identify the mode and the two registers that form the address.
quiz.a: Indexed mode. The address is A + DPTR, and the byte is read from code memory.

quiz.q: What does @R0 mean in 8051 MOV A,@R0?
quiz.a: @R0 means the memory location whose address is held in register R0. R0 is a pointer, not the data.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern load-store designs use base plus immediate offset. ARM (A32) allows a shift on the index register inside the load/store, and x86-64 scales the index by 1, 2, 4 or 8 with the SIB byte. RISC-V keeps it simple: a load or store uses base plus immediate offset only, so the compiler must compute the byte offset of an array element with a separate shift or multiply. Security research looks at addressing modes for memory safety, for example pointer authentication and bounds checks. Search for 'RISC-V addressing modes' or 'x86-64 SIB byte' to see how the encoding works.
